'''David D.''' "'''Deacon'''" '''Jones''' (December 9, 1938 – June 3, 2013) was an American professional [[American football|football]] [[defensive end]] who played in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for 14 seasons. He played for the [[Los Angeles Rams]], [[San Diego Chargers]], and [[Washington Redskins]]. He was inducted into the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] in 1980.

Jones specialized in [[Quarterback sack|sacks]]. Nicknamed "'''the Secretary of Defense'''", Jones is considered one of the greatest defensive players ever.<ref name=jones>{{cite web | work=Deacon Jones Foundation | url=https://www.deaconjones.com/about-deacon.php | title=About Deacon | access-date=July 18, 2008}}</ref>  The ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'' called Jones the "most valuable Ram of all time", and former Rams head coach [[George Allen (coach)|George Allen]] called him the "greatest defensive end of modern football".<ref name=jones />

'''Dedrick Roper''' (born July 31, 1981) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Northwood Timberwolves football|Northwood Timberwolves]].

Roper was born in [[Detroit, Michigan|Detroit]], [[Michigan]] and  raised in [[Milpitas, California|Milpitas]], [[California]]. He began his NFL career with the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]], and played for the [[St. Louis Rams]] for all of one week before the Eagles signed him in [[2005 NFL season|2005 season]].  He was cut by the Eagles prior to the 2006 season and spent time on the practice squad.  He was re-signed later in the season due to injuries to the defense.

'''Dadrian LaBreece '''"'''Dee'''"''' Brown''' (born May 12, 1978) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He went to high school at [[Lake Brantley High School]], where he played [[quarterback]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Syracuse Orange football|Syracuse Orange]] and was moved to running back with [[Donovan McNabb]] as their quarterback. Brown was selected by the [[Carolina Panthers]] in the sixth round (175th overall) of the [[2001 NFL draft]].
<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dee Brown Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/B/BrowDe02.htm |access-date=2025-10-07 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=2001 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2001/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-17 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>

After his playing career, Brown went into coaching, initially serving as a special assistant for the [[Denver Broncos]]. He then spent several years as a high school coach before joining the college ranks in 2021 as offensive coordinator for [[NCAA Division II]] [[Livingstone College|Livingstone]]. After one season, he moved to [[NCAA Division I Football Championship Subdivision|Division I FCS]] [[Campbell Fighting Camels football|Campbell]] as running backs coach.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://gocamels.com/sports/football/roster/coaches/dee-brown/909 |title=Dee Brown |publisher=Campbell Fighting Camels |accessdate=March 1, 2022}}</ref>

'''Dean Wells''' (July 20, 1970 – April 3, 2025) was an American professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) from 1993 to 2001. 

Wells played [[college football]] for the [[Kentucky Wildcats football|Kentucky Wildcats]].<ref>[http://www.nfl.com/player/deanwells/2503591/profile NFL.com profile]</ref> He holds the school record for most sacks in a single game, recording five against Indiana in 1992,<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Condotta |first=Bob |date=2025-04-04 |title=Former Seahawks tackles leader dies after battle with cancer |url=https://www.seattletimes.com/sports/seahawks/former-seahawks-linebacker-dean-wells-reportedly-dies-at-54/ |access-date=2025-04-04 |website=The Seattle Times |language=en-US}}</ref> as well as single-season sack record with 10.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Roush |first=Nick |date=2025-04-04 |title=Dean Wells, Homegrown Kentucky Football Standout, Passes Away at 54 |url=https://www.on3.com/teams/kentucky-wildcats/news/dean-wells-homegrown-kentucky-football-standout-passes-away-at-54/ |access-date=2025-04-04 |website=On3 |language=en}}</ref> Wells was selected in the fourth round of the [[1993 NFL draft]] by the [[Seattle Seahawks]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=1993 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1993/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-31 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> and played five seasons for the team, leading the defense in tackles in 1996.<ref name=":1" /> He signed as a free agent with the [[Carolina Panthers]] in 1999 and spent three seasons with the team.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Former Panthers linebacker Dean Wells dies at 54 |url=https://www.panthers.com/news/former-panthers-linebacker-dean-wells-dies-at-54 |access-date=2025-04-04 |website=www.panthers.com |language=en-US}}</ref> 

Wells ended his career with 529 tackles, 2.5 sacks, six forced fumbles, four fumble recoveries, and three interceptions.<ref name=":2" /> He died from [[acute lymphoblastic leukemia]] on April 3, 2025, at the age of 54.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Roush |first=Nick |date=2025-04-04 |title=Dean Wells, Homegrown Kentucky Football Standout, Passes Away at 54 |url=https://www.on3.com/teams/kentucky-wildcats/news/dean-wells-homegrown-kentucky-football-standout-passes-away-at-54/ |access-date=2025-04-04 |website=On3 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="u756">{{cite web | last= | first= | title=Former NFL linebacker Dean Wells dies at 54 after two-year battle with cancer | website=The Times of India | date=5 April 2025 | url=https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/sports/nfl/news/former-nfl-linebacker-dean-wells-dies-at-54-after-two-year-battle-with-cancer/articleshow/119992536.cms | access-date=5 April 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Dye |first1=Natasha |title=Former Carolina Panthers Linebacker Dean Wells Dead at 54 |url=https://people.com/former-nfl-linebacker-dean-wells-dead-54-11709632 |website=[[People (magazine)|People]] |access-date=7 April 2025 |date=4 April 2025}}</ref>

'''William David "Dee" Hardison''' (May 2, 1956 – April 21, 2018) was an American professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[defensive end]] and [[defensive tackle]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Buffalo Bills]] (1978–1980), [[New York Giants]] (1982–1985), [[San Diego Chargers]] (1986–1987) and [[Kansas City Chiefs]] (1988).  He played [[college football]] for the [[North Carolina Tar Heels football|North Carolina Tar Heels]].

Hardison helped the Bills win the 1980 [[AFC East]] Division and helped the Bills defense lead the NFL in fewest passing yards allowed in 1978 and the AFC in 1979 and 1980 and NFL in fewest total yards allowed in 1980 and the Chiefs lead the NFL in fewest passing yards allowed in 1988.

In ten seasons, Hardison had nine [[Quarterback sack|sacks]].

Hardison died on April 21, 2018, at the age of 61.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.fayobserver.com/sports/20180422/ex-hobbton-unc-football-star-dee-hardison-dies-at-61|title=Ex-Hobbton, UNC football star Dee Hardison dies at 61|publisher=fayobserver.com|author=Sammy Batten|date=2018-04-22|accessdate=2018-04-22}}</ref>

'''Dedrick Allen Dodge''' (born June 14, 1967) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Safety (gridiron football position)|safety]] for eight seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) from 1991 to 1998. He played [[college football]] for the [[Florida State Seminoles football|Florida State Seminoles]]. Dodge is a two-time [[Super Bowl]] champion. He played in [[Super Bowl XXIX]] for the [[San Francisco 49ers]] and in [[Super Bowl XXXII]] for the [[Denver Broncos]]. He also played for the [[London Monarchs]] in the inaugural season of the [[NFL Europe|World League of American Football]] (WLAF); London won the first World Bowl that year, meaning that Dodge has three pro football championship rings. After his playing career, he became a coach. 

Dodge played [[high school football]] at [[East Brunswick High School]] in [[East Brunswick, New Jersey]] and [[Mulberry High School (Mulberry, Florida)|Mulberry High School]] in [[Mulberry, Florida]].<ref>[http://www.profootballarchives.com/dodg00200.html Dedrick Dodge] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150908092850/http://www.profootballarchives.com/dodg00200.html |date=September 8, 2015 }}, The Pro Football Archives. Accessed February 5, 2016. "High School: East Brunswick (NJ); Mulberry (FL)"</ref>

Dodge spent two seasons as the head football coach at Mulberry Senior High School. According to ''[[The Ledger]]'' of Lakeland, Dodge previously coached a year at Evangel Christian in [[Lakeland, Florida]], leading the team to an 11–3 record and a state title in 2005. He then coached a year at Victory Christian after Evangel folded and led the Storm to a 10–4 record with some of Evangel's former players.

Victory finished state runner-up in 2005, losing to Tallahassee FAMU in the 1B state title game.
Dodge has returned to his home in [[Locust Grove, Georgia]], about 30 miles south of [[Atlanta]], where he maintained a home in Georgia since 2007 after he began coaching at [[Fort Valley State University]] as an assistant.  Dodge previously coached in Polk County at Victory Christian, Mulberry and Evangel Christian, where he won a state title in 2005.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Fuoco |first1=Roy |title=Davidson takes over at Ridge for homesick Dodge |url=https://www.theledger.com/story/sports/high-school/football/2020/09/08/davidson-takes-over-ridge-homesick-dodge/5749657002/ |website=The Ledger |access-date=1 February 2021}}</ref>
